pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: When Factorial(3) runs, what does the call stack look like at its deepest point — and why does breaking the base case end in a stack overflow?
expected_points: each call pushes a frame holding its own private copy of n; frames pop in reverse order as results return
at the deepest point frames for n=3, 2, 1, 0 are all live, each waiting on the call above it
with no reachable base case frames pile up until the stack limit is hit and the program dies (in Go a fatal error, not a recoverable panic)

questions.prompt: New problem, no code yet: count how many files live in a folder, including all nested subfolders. What is the base case, and what is the recursive case?
expected_points: base case: a folder with no subfolders — return its own file count
recursive case: this folder's file count plus the recursive count of each subfolder
identifies both cases from the problem statement before writing code, and checks that recursion makes progress toward the base case

questions.prompt: Trace Factorial(4) by hand: draw the stack frames as they are pushed, then walk the unwinding and say what each frame returns.
expected_points: winding: frames for 4, 3, 2, 1, 0 pushed in order, each with its own n
unwinding: 0 returns 1, then 1, 2, 6, 24 as each frame multiplies its n by the returned value
keeps the two phases and each frame's variables clearly separate

questions.prompt: In your Sum, how does the shape of the code mirror the shape of a Node? And what would happen if Children could contain a cycle back to an ancestor?
expected_points: the nil check is the base case; one recursive call per child mirrors 'a value plus nested nodes'
recursion handles nesting of unknown depth where a plain loop is awkward
a cycle means no progress toward the base case — infinite recursion ending in stack overflow

questions.prompt: Your SumIterative swaps recursion for a slice used as a stack. Why does it survive the million-node chain when a recursive version dies, and when would you reach for iteration first?
expected_points: the explicit stack lives on the heap and grows with append — bounded by memory, not the goroutine stack limit
recursion costs one frame per level and Go does not optimize tail calls
prefer iteration for unbounded or user-controlled depth and flat linear data; prefer recursion for naturally nested data

questions.prompt: Naive recursive fibonacci makes two calls per level. Roughly how does its running time grow with n, and what exactly is being wasted?
expected_points: the call tree roughly doubles per level — exponential, about O(2^n) in the Big-O growth classes
the same subproblems (fib(3), fib(2), …) are recomputed many times
the definition is correct but repeats work — seeing the repeated subtrees is the skill; the fix comes in the dynamic-programming lesson
